The two verses given seams read כָּל יְמֵי — 6:5 כָּל יְמֵי֙ נֶ֣דֶר נִזְר֔וֹ, 6:6 כָּל יְמֵ֥י הַזִּיר֖וֹ — while the two passed over read כֹּ֖ל יְמֵ֣י נִזְר֑וֹ at 6:4 and 6:8. So the hair prohibition at 6:5 is properly its own provision, syntactically parallel to the corpse prohibition at 6:6 and distinct from the recapitulations that bracket them. Verdict reflects the text rather than the draft's rationale, which never mentions the distinction.

preserved_peer_crosscheck.assessment: This is one of the task's flagged questions and I worked it from the Hebrew myself rather than taking either primary's word for it. LF's challenge (LF-M8-Num-041-1) is right that no fresh 'Yahweh spoke to Moses' formula separates the wine, hair, and corpse prohibitions -- all three sit inside the single speech opened once at 6:1-2, and LF is also right that this reviewer's own principle at M8-Num-044 ('single unbroken purpose... no change of officiant, location, or governing formula') would, applied evenly, merge 6:1-8 rather than split it three ways. OL's rebuttal leans on a real vocalization distinction -- 6:4 and 6:8 read כֹּל (holam) while 6:5 and 6:6 read כָּל (qamats) -- and I confirmed this directly in Num_oshb.txt; the forms do differ exactly as OL describes. But I also checked whether this alternation actually carries the 'recapitulation vs. new-provision' function OL assigns it, by tracing the same כֹּל/כָּל pair elsewhere in this corpus, and it does not hold up: 1:3's command clause reads כָּל יֹצֵא צָבָא while every one of the twelve near-identical tribal entries at 1:20-42 reads כֹּל יֹצֵא צָבָא in the same syntactic slot -- a pure formulaic constant across all twelve entries, not a discourse-level open/close signal, since none of those twelve occurrences is a 'closing recap' of anything. That comparison undercuts OL's specific argument for why 041 should stay separate from 042, even though OL's citation of the actual forms is accurate. On the substantive question, I side with the challenge: this reads more naturally as one register of three co-equal prohibitions under one vow-declaration, closer in kind to the six wrapped objects M8-Num-024 correctly keeps merged than to the ch.3 speech-formula sequence it was compared against.

preserved_primary_reviews.rationale: I don't think this single verse earns free-standing status, and the decision's own rejected alternative is the stronger reading. Every other short travel/arrival notice in this book's recent stretch is treated as attached material rather than a free-standing decision: the Hazeroth notice at 11:35 closes the quail episode (M8-Num-081), and the Paran notice at 12:16 closes the Miriam episode (M8-Num-085) -- in both cases because a preceding narrative scene existed for the notice to close. Here that pattern breaks down structurally: the material immediately before 20:1 is timeless casuistic legislation (the red heifer/corpse-contact law), which has no camp or scene for an arrival notice to close, so v.1's 'came into the wilderness of Zin...stayed in Kadesh' cannot function as a closing bridge the way the other notices do. It can only be read as opening material, and Kadesh is confirmed as the setting for everything through at least v.13 and arguably through v.21 ('Moses sent messengers from Kadesh,' 20:14). The decision claims 'no causal link to the following complaint stated in the text itself,' but the tight juxtaposition -- Miriam's death notice immediately followed by 'there was no water for the congregation' with no intervening material -- is exactly the kind of implied narrative sequencing this book uses elsewhere without spelling out causation explicitly (compare how the quail plague follows directly from the people's gluttony with no stated causal clause at 11:33). The verse's content is also too thin to justify independent status: two bare clauses (arrival, death-and-burial) with no developed scene, dialogue, or etiology of its own, unlike every other unit in this cluster.

That mismatch is a real feature of the Hebrew and not a transmission artefact in either witness. None of it disturbs the edges, which are setumah-bounded on both sides. The drafter's stated principle, following the register's own accounting rather than smoothing it, is the correct instinct for a candidate-stage decision.

preserved_primary_reviews.rationale: The decision's own rejected-alternative asks the right question and then declines to answer it in favor of the more consistent reading: "one could question whether it deserves its own decision at all" (Dan names only one sub-clan of the whole tribe, the thinnest genealogical content of any entry in the register), before falling back on "the register itself treats Dan as a complete, self-contained entry." preserved_primary_reviews.rationale: Frame present at both ends, setumah in both witnesses at 26:43 before and 26:47 after. The interesting judgement is the Serah notice at v.46, and the drafter distinguishes it from the Zelophehad notice on the right ground rather than a convenient one: both are bare naming clauses embedded in a clan list, neither has an introducing formula, and the difference lies in what the later text does with them, not in their form here. Since the campaign's criterion is the register's own frame, form is what should govern, and on form both stay internal. I looked at 26:45 as a possible internal break because it descends to Beriah's sons; it continues the same לְ-plus-gentilic chain.

frozen_row_v0.boundary_rationale: זֹאת עֲבֹדַת בְּנֵי קְהָת ("this is the service of the sons of Kohath") opens one governing clause applied identically across each sacred object -- ark, table, lampstand, golden altar, other vessels, bronze altar -- with the recurring cover-and-carry refrain, וְשָׁמוּ בַּדָּיו ("and put in its poles"), binding the six objects into one continuous wrapping instruction rather than six independent commands.
frozen_row_v0.strongest_rejected_alternative: Each object could be split into its own decision the way this book's furniture-panel material sometimes is, since ark, table, lampstand, and altars are materially distinct items; but every object here is wrapped under the identical opening formula and closed with the identical pole-insertion refrain with no new principle introduced object to object, so I read this as one uniform procedural register.

preserved_primary_reviews.rationale: As a unit this is coherent: זֹ֛את עֲבֹדַ֥ת בְּנֵי קְהָ֖ת בְּאֹ֣הֶל מוֹעֵ֑ד functions as a heading, and what follows is an ordered wrapping procedure in weqatal (וּבָ֨א, וְנָ֥תְנוּ, וּפָֽרְשׂ֞וּ, וְלָקְח֣וּ, וְדִשְּׁנ֖וּ, וְנָתְנ֣וּ) covering ark, table, lampstand, golden altar, vessels and bronze altar in turn. The זֹאת עֲבֹדַת formula is a real rubric-class opener. What I cannot endorse is that this formula is honoured as a boundary here and passed over at 4:24 and 4:31; that asymmetry is registered as a challenge on M8-Num-028 rather than here, because this instance is the one the text most clearly supports.

preserved_primary_reviews.rationale: Checked against WEB: v.4's opening formula 'This is the service of the sons of Kohath' governs six objects (ark, table, lampstand, golden altar, vessels, bronze altar), each closed by the same cover-then-carry pattern -- though the closing refrain is not perfectly uniform: four objects close on 'put in its poles' (vv.6, 8, 11, 14) while two (lampstand, vessels) close on 'put it on the frame' (vv.10, 12), a minor imprecision in the boundary rationale's phrasing that does not affect the underlying call. No object introduces a new legal principle, so keeping all six as one register rather than splitting per object is the right application of the over-split test -- the same logic that correctly merges the ch.7 register.

preserved_peer_crosscheck.assessment: The זֹאת עֲבֹדַת heading at 4:4 does open a coherent six-object wrapping procedure with no new legal principle introduced object to object, so merging rather than splitting by furniture item is right. LF is correct in its own review that the closing refrain is not perfectly uniform ('put in its poles' vs 'put it on the frame'), but that is a minor descriptive imprecision, not a boundary problem. The substantive issue with this formula's treatment is not internal to this decision but is about its inconsistent application at 4:24 and 4:31 -- addressed at M8-Num-028.
